bodies.linkedin:
Some OCR technology claims to capture 99.91% of data.

This evolution began in 1914 when Emanuel Goldberg developed a machine that converted characters into standard telegraph code. By 1931, he was granted US Patent number 1,838,389 for a statistical machine used to search microfilm archives.

Modern systems have moved far beyond those early experiments. Today, tools like PaddleOCR support over 80 languages, while specialized processes like binarization convert images to black-and-white to separate text from the background. Other systems use the Levenshtein Distance algorithm to optimize results during post-processing.

Efficiency remains a priority for large-scale operations. The New York Times uses a tool called Document Helper to process up to 5,400 pages per hour. Despite these advancements, OCR systems still encounter 'scannos' when processing complex documents.

Accuracy is the ultimate metric for machine-encoded text.

bodies.thread:
Some OCR technology claims to capture 99.91% of data.

Errors in this process are sometimes referred to as 'scannos'.

A character error rate of 1% (99% accuracy) may result in an error rate of 5% or worse if word context is not used.

The Levenshtein Distance algorithm is used in OCR post-processing to optimize results.

Near-neighbor analysis uses co-occurrence frequencies to correct OCR errors.

Total OCR accuracy can be achieved through human review or Data Dictionary Authentication.

Machines have evolved from early telegraphic experiments to systems that now interpret and act upon visual text from diverse sources.
